title: Tactics Basics
description: Learn the first tricks every player needs: forks, pins, skewers, discovered attacks, loose pieces and smart trades.

steps.intro: A knight on c7 attacks e8 and a8. The king is on e8 and the rook is on a8.

moves.comment: The knight gives check to the king. It also attacks the rook.
The king must deal with the check.
Now the knight takes the rook for free.

steps.intro: White to move. The knight on d5 can jump to c7.
Look at the knight on c7.

hints: Jump with your knight to a square next to the king and the rook.
steps.intro: Play the fork as White. Then win the rook.

points: A fork is one move that attacks two things at once
Knights are great at forks because they jump and attack in an odd shape
Ask students to count which squares the knight on d5 can reach
mistakes: Forgetting that the forking piece can be captured
Forking two pawns when a bigger fork was there
questions: Why can the black player only fix one problem?
Which squares does a knight on c7 attack?

steps.intro: Before you play a fork, name the two pieces you attack.

moves.comment: Check! The knight also attacks the queen.
White wins the queen.

hints: Jump to e7. It gives check and attacks the queen on c8.
steps.intro: White to move. Find the fork that wins the queen.

moves.comment: Check! The knight also attacks the rook on a1.
Black wins the rook.

hints: Jump to c2. It gives check and attacks the rook on a1.
steps.intro: Black to move. Find the fork.

points: Have students name the two targets before they name the move
A check plus an attack is the strongest fork because the king must move
mistakes: Moving the knight to a square where a pawn can take it
Looking only at captures and missing quiet knight jumps
questions: What are the two targets?
Can Black take the knight after it lands?

steps.intro: A pawn can fork two pieces too, and pawns are worth the least.

moves.comment: The pawn steps forward and attacks both knights.
One knight runs away.
The pawn takes the other knight. White has won a piece.

steps.intro: White to move. Look at the two black knights.

moves.comment: The pawn attacks both knights.
Black wins a knight.

hints: Push the pawn from c5 to c4.
steps.intro: Black to move. Find the pawn fork.

points: Pawns attack diagonally forward
A pawn fork wins a piece because pawns are worth the least
Check that nothing can capture the pawn after it lands
mistakes: Forgetting which way a pawn captures
Pushing the pawn to a square where it can be taken
questions: Which two squares does a pawn on c5 attack?
Why is it hard for Black to stop a pawn fork?

steps.intro: The bishop on b4 attacks along the line to the king. If the knight leaves, the king is in check, so the move is not allowed.

moves.comment: The bishop attacks the knight on f6. Behind the knight is the black queen on d8.

steps.intro: Watch White pin a knight in a real opening.
This is an absolute pin. The black bishop attacks the knight on c3, and the white king is behind it.
Look at the line from the bishop to the king.

moves.comment: The knight is pinned to the queen.

steps.intro: White to move. Pin the knight on f6 against the queen.

hints: Open the game with a pawn in the middle.
Your last move is the bishop pin on g5.
steps.intro: Play the moves that lead to the pin.

points: Absolute pin: the piece behind is the king, so the pinned piece cannot legally move
Relative pin: the piece behind is something valuable but not the king, so moving is legal but costly
Bishops, rooks and queens make pins because they attack along lines
mistakes: Thinking a relative pin means the piece cannot move
Forgetting the square behind the pinned piece must hold the target
questions: Which piece is the pinned piece?
What is hiding behind it?

steps.intro: A pinned piece cannot run away, so attack it.

moves.comment: The pawn attacks the pinned knight. The knight cannot move.
Black unpins it, but there is no time to save the knight.
White wins a knight for a pawn.

steps.intro: The bishop pins the knight on c6 to the king on e8.

moves.comment: The pawn attacks the pinned knight. It cannot move away.
Black wins a knight for a pawn.

hints: Push the pawn from d5 to d4 to attack the pinned knight.
steps.intro: Black to move. The white knight on c3 is pinned. Win it.

points: A pinned piece is a target because it cannot run away
Attack it with something smaller than it
Here the pinned knight even attacks the d4 pawn but cannot take it
mistakes: Attacking the pinned piece with a big piece that can be captured
Forgetting that the enemy king can step aside and end the pin
questions: Why can the black knight not run away?
What small piece can attack it?

steps.intro: The rook on d8 is behind the king on the same file. When the king steps aside, the white rook takes it.

moves.comment: The rook gives check along the d-file.
The king has to move out of the way.
The rook behind the king is now attacked and White takes it.

steps.intro: White to move. The black king and rook stand on the same file.
Black must answer the check.

moves.comment: Check! The black rook on a5 is behind the king.
White wins the rook.

hints: Move it to h5. It gives check along the fifth rank.
steps.intro: White to move. Find the skewer.

hints: Give check with your rook along the rank.
Play the rook to h5, then take the rook on a5.
steps.intro: Play the skewer as White.

points: A skewer is like a pin turned around: the big piece is in front
The front piece must move, then you take the piece behind
Rooks, bishops and queens make skewers
mistakes: Mixing up a pin and a skewer
Skewering when the king can step to a square that defends the piece behind
questions: Which piece is in front?
What is the difference between a pin and a skewer?

steps.intro: In a discovered attack, one piece moves away and uncovers an attack from the piece behind it.

moves.comment: The knight takes the queen. Now the rook on e1 gives check.
Black takes the knight, but White has won a queen for a knight.

steps.intro: The knight on e5 blocks the rook on e1. The rook points at the black king.
The knight is about to move.

moves.comment: The knight takes the queen and the rook gives check.

steps.intro: Black to move. The rook on e8 is hiding behind the knight. Find the discovered check that wins the queen.

hints: Capture the queen with your knight.
steps.intro: Play the discovered check as White.

points: One piece steps out of the way and uncovers an attack by a piece behind it
The moving piece can make its own threat at the same time
A discovered check is the strongest kind because the king must answer it
mistakes: Moving the front piece without checking what the back piece now attacks
Forgetting that the moving piece can be captured afterwards
questions: Which piece is hiding behind the knight?
Why is a check so hard to ignore?

steps.intro: A piece with no defender is hanging. The other side can capture it without losing anything back.

moves.comment: It is White's turn, so the queen takes the bishop for free.

steps.intro: The black bishop attacks the white queen. But nothing defends the bishop!

moves.comment: Nothing defends the knight, so White wins it for free.

steps.intro: White to move. One black piece is hanging. Take it.

hints: Look for a black piece that nothing defends.
steps.intro: Take the hanging knight as White.

points: Hanging means no friendly piece defends it
Always ask: what can the opponent take for free?
Check your own pieces as well as theirs
mistakes: Moving a piece and leaving another undefended
Not noticing that an attacked piece also attacks your piece
questions: Which pieces defend this one?
Who moves first, and does that change the answer?

steps.intro: Before you take a piece, ask: can it take back?

moves.comment: The queen takes the knight.
The bishop takes back. White lost a queen for a knight. That is a bad trade.

steps.intro: The white queen attacks the knight on d5. But the bishop on c6 defends the knight.
White's queen attacks the pawn on e5.

moves.comment: The bishop on g4 had no defender.

hints: The bishop on g4 has no defender.
steps.intro: White to move. One capture is safe and one is a mistake. Find the safe one.

points: Before you capture, count who can take back
A defended piece is not always safe to capture, but a trade of equal value can be fine
A queen should almost never take a defended pawn or minor piece
mistakes: Taking a pawn with the queen when a piece guards the pawn
Only looking at the piece you capture and not at what happens next
questions: Who can take back if I capture here?
How many points would I lose?

steps.intro: Ask three questions: What does my opponent attack? Is my target defended? Is the trade good for me?

moves.comment: This takes a knight, but the bishop on c3 defends it.
Black lost a queen for a knight. The three questions would have stopped this.

steps.intro: Black to move. The white bishop on g5 attacks the black queen.

moves.comment: The queen saves itself and wins a bishop.

hints: Take the bishop on g5. Nothing defends it.
steps.intro: Black to move. Use the three questions, then find the safe capture.

points: Make the three questions a habit: What does my opponent attack? Is my target defended? Is this trade good for me?
Ask them out loud every move in class
Works for both colors
mistakes: Grabbing the first free-looking capture
Forgetting to check what the opponent attacks
questions: What does the white bishop attack?
Is the knight on d4 defended?

lessons.title: How much is each piece worth?

steps.intro: Giving 3 points and getting 5 points means you come out 2 points ahead.
Count the points. Pawn 1. Knight 3. Bishop 3. Rook 5. Queen 9. The king is priceless.

moves.comment: The rook can take back, but you gave 1 point and won 9.

hints: Take the biggest piece. Capture on e5.
steps.intro: White to move. The pawn can take the rook or the queen. Take the one worth more.

points: Pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9
The king cannot be traded, so it has no number
The numbers are a guide, not a law: position and attacks matter too
mistakes: Trading a rook for a bishop without a reason
Forgetting that the numbers are only a guide
questions: Which is worth more, a bishop or a rook?
How many pawns is a queen worth?

steps.intro: Trading up means you give a smaller piece to win a bigger one.

moves.comment: White gives a bishop (3).
White took a rook (5). White gained 2 points in the trade.

steps.intro: The black rook on f7 is defended by the king. But a rook is worth more than a bishop.

moves.comment: A pawn (1) wins a bishop (3). Even if Black takes back, White gains 2 points in the trade.

steps.intro: White to move. Trade your smallest piece for a bigger one.

moves.comment: A knight (3) wins a rook (5). The pawn takes back, but White gains 2 points and the material is now equal.

steps.intro: White to move. The rook is defended by a pawn. Is the trade still good?

hints: Look at the bishop and the rook.
Play the bishop to f7 with check.
steps.intro: Play the trade as White.

points: Trading up means giving a smaller piece to win a bigger one
Even if the enemy takes back, you still gain points
Look for captures where your piece is worth less than the target
mistakes: Trading down: giving a bigger piece for a smaller one
Trading up into a position where you are checkmated
questions: How many points did we give?
How many points did we get?
